Start with one box.

One process holds every socket, every message and every row. It is simple, and it works until it doesn't.

"It's time for web servers to handle ten thousand clients simultaneously." That was 1999.

one thread per client tops out

Stop asking. Get told.

Polling asks on a timer and mostly hears "nothing new". Long polling holds each request open. A WebSocket upgrades once and stays open both ways.

Polling
Long polling
WebSocket

Long polling's worst case is over three network transits per message, and 30 seconds is the safer timeout.

Scale up before you scale out.

Event-driven I/O lets one box hold millions of mostly idle sockets. Measure the box you have before buying more.

One message, many sockets.

Gateways subscribe to the channels their users are in. A pub/sub bus copies each message to every interested gateway.

Plain Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once: if a subscriber drops, that message is gone.

Write it down, in order.

Chat is write-heavy and read newest-first. Give every message a sortable ID and partition by conversation and time.

Spread the load. Cache the answers.

Consistent hashing moves only one slice of keys when a node joins. A cache absorbs the hot reads.

Each key lives on N nodes. Reads and writes need R and W of them, with R + W > N. Dynamo often ran (3, 2, 2).

peak database queries during a thundering herd
no leases: 17K/s
memcache leases: 1.3K/s

Deliver at least once. Apply exactly once.

Networks lose acks, so senders retry. Tag each send with an ID and let the server ignore repeats.

Kafka is at-least-once by default. Messenger's Iris keeps a totally ordered queue with a pointer per device; it cut data use by about 40%.

Plan for the bad day.

Retries multiply. Retry at one layer, budget it, shed what can wait, and treat push as a wake-up call.

243× load

A 10% retry budget keeps the worst case near 1.1×.
